newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Help Bulgaria to help itself, president urges EU.
newsitem.headline: Help Bulgaria to help itself, president urges EU.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president, his country mired in a 24th consecutive day of strikes and rallies, urged the European Union on Wednesday to help his country get out of its dire economic crisis.

As workers around Bulgaria kept up pressure on the ex-communist ruling Socialists in a protest over the country's economic crisis and to back opposition demands for early elections, Petar Stoyanov said the EU should help Bulgaria to help itself.
"The shortest, most direct course to help Bulgaria to enable her to pay its debts is to help us to help ourselves," he told the European Parliament's foreign affairs committee.
"We would appeal to you to show understanding."
He said more direct EU investment and quick talks on EU accession were important to meet the crisis and prevent the country slipping backwards in democratic terms.
He acknowledged that the country was not ready for EU entry talks, but said any delay on the EU side would make Bulgaria's citizens lose faith in the process.

"Unless they start without delay the Bulgarian people will lose their confidence in adoption of democratic values," he said, adding that Bulgarians felt they were regarded by the western bloc as "second class Europeans."
Bulgaria is one of 10 eastern European countries to have applied for EU membership, but is thought unlikely to be among the first group with whom the EU is expected to open talks next year.
Stoyanov also urged help in retrieving $2 billion owed by Iraq.

Blaming the former government for the crisis, Stoyanov said that Bulgaria had shown itself to be "a good European pupil" and had suffered from applying an embargo on Serbia and being cut off from the rest of Europe by the fighting in ex-Yugoslavia.
After failing to find a compromise between the warring political factions, Stoyanov on Tuesday asked Nikolai Dobrev, the interior minister of the Socialist party, to form a new government.

The opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) said it would suspend its boycott of the 240-seat parliament to try to stop Dobrev from winning approval for a government. Although the Socialists have an absolute majority, the UDF hopes defections could stop Dobrev.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov had to give the mandate to the Socialists -- parliament's biggest party and the caretaker government since Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21.
The opposition wants an immediate general election, while the Socialists are proposing polls in the autumn, more than a year before their mandate expires in December 1998.
